extracted.subtask_short: identifying vultures in the United States
extracted.subtask_description: A short field‑guide style article describing the three vulture species found in the U.S., with identification features, behaviors, ranges, size measurements, sounds, nesting and conservation notes to help readers find and recognize each species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turkey Vulture identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Turkey Vulture (Cathartes aura) is all black, with a bald red head and a pinkish bill. In flight look for a large raptor soaring in wobbly circles with wings raised high enough to look like the letter 'V.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visible features plus behavior: they soar low (V wing posture) to smell for food. They prefer fresh carrion, are often seen along roadsides, and produce only a hissing sound. Typical measurements: Length 25–32 in (64–81 cm); Weight 2–5 lbs (0.8–2.4 kg); Wingspan 63–72 in (160–183 cm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Vulture identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Black Vultures (Coragyps atratus) are covered in black feathers with a bald black head and show silver feathers on the underside of their wings; they are shorter and more compact than Turkey Vultures and display silvery wingtips in flight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from Turkey Vultures by head color and wing underside (black head + silvery tips vs red head + gray underside), plus posture. Black Vultures are common in the southern U.S., nest in stumps/caves/brush/hollow trees (no nesting material), are monogamous and aggressive at carcasses (sometimes chase off Turkey Vultures), and make grunting/hissing noises. Measurements: Length 22–29 in (56–74 cm); Weight 3½–6½ lbs (1.6–3 kg); Wingspan 51–66 in (1.3–1.7 m).

rubrics_metrics.name: California Condor identification & conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: The California Condor (Gymnogyps californianus) is the largest U.S. bird, predominantly black with a white underwing and a head whose color ranges from yellow/orange/pink/purple/blue to red; eyes are deep red.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condors were extinct in the wild (captured in 1987) and reintroduced via captive breeding beginning 1991; population figures (March 2020) cited: 337 wild, 181 captive. Key conservation threats: lead poisoning (from unretrieved shot animals), poaching, habitat loss, and low reproductive rate (one egg, late maturity). Behaviorally they ride thermals (can soar near 15,000 ft), travel long distances (up to ~150 miles searching for food), can gulp ~4 lbs at once, and are mostly silent (hissing/throat‑clearing). Measurements: Height 36–42 in (91–107 cm); Weight 17–25 lbs; Wingspan 114 in (290 cm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flight posture and soaring behavior as identification cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Flight posture and soaring style differ by species: Turkey Vultures fly with wings raised (V shape) and 'wobbly circles' to glide low and smell for carrion; Black Vultures display silvery wingtips; Condors have almost straight frontlines and 'finger‑feathers' on wingtips that make them sensitive to thermals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe wing angle, wingtip shape, and underside coloration while birds are soaring — these are reliable field marks for separating species at a distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head and plumage coloration as field marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Head coloration and underwing/underside plumage are key: Turkey Vulture = bald red head, grayish underside; Black Vulture = bald black head, silvery undersides at wingtips; California Condor = variable colorful head and white underwing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use head color and underwing contrast (especially while soaring) to tell species apart; check head color, skin tone, and the amount of pale/white on the underwing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size and measurements for confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each species has characteristic length, weight, and wingspan ranges provided: Turkey Vulture (25–32 in; 2–5 lbs; 63–72 in), Black Vulture (22–29 in; 3½–6½ lbs; 51–66 in), California Condor (height 36–42 in; weight 17–25 lbs; wingspan 114 in).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use size estimates (when possible) to corroborate visual identification, especially when plumage marks are ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding behavior and sense of smell
rubrics_metrics.description: Turkey Vultures use a highly developed sense of smell (can detect dead meat from 8 miles/13 km away) and prefer fresh carrion; Black Vultures primarily eat carrion but will kill animals to eat fresh meat; Condors can travel far to find food and gulp large quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feeding behavior helps predict where to find species (e.g., Turkey Vultures along roadsides; Black Vultures in fields/near Turkey Vultures). Note aggressive behavior of Black Vultures at carcasses and condors' ability to cover great distances for food.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nesting habits and parental care
rubrics_metrics.description: Black Vultures nest on the ground in stumps, caves, thickets, brush piles, or hollow trees without nesting material and are monogamous, with parents feeding chicks up to 8 months; California Condors produce one egg and captive programs removed first eggs to encourage second egg-laying, raising chicks with puppets to avoid imprinting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nesting location and parental strategies are useful for understanding species biology and for conservation/monitoring efforts (e.g., searching likely nest sites, recognizing human‑assisted breeding practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocalization (limited) as an identifying trait
rubrics_metrics.description: Vultures are mostly silent: Turkey Vultures produce only hissing; Black Vultures make grunting and hissing noises; Condors produce hissing and a throat‑clearing sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of song and presence of simple hisses/grunts can help confirm vulture observations; do not expect melodic calls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral defenses and hygiene adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: Vultures have featherless heads and necks to stay clean inside carrion; they defecate on their legs to cool blood and regulate temperature; when too heavy to fly, they may projectile vomit to lose weight and escape predators. Their stomach acid protects them from pathogens like rabies, plague, botulism, distemper, and anthrax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These behaviors explain why vultures are adapted to scavenging and may be observed performing unusual actions (leg‑soiling, vomiting) near carcasses — useful context for field observers and for interpreting behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range, habitat, and when/where to look
rubrics_metrics.description: Turkey Vultures are widespread across the U.S. and commonly found along roadsides and open countryside; Black Vultures are found in the southern U.S. in forested and open areas and often roost in dense forests; California Condors are localized to reintroduction areas in California, Arizona, Utah and parts of Baja California/Mexico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult local range maps and seasonal events (e.g., 'Buzzard Day' migrations) to know where and when to look for each species; habitat and regional presence strongly influence chances of encountering a species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation threats and human impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Key threats cited for California Condors include lead poisoning (from unretrieved shot animals), poaching, habitat loss, low reproductive rate (one egg), and late sexual maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conservation actions implied: reduce lead in the environment (e.g., collect carcasses or stop using lead ammunition), habitat protection, and captive breeding/reintroduction programs; population figures and historical recovery illustrate management needs.
